description.value: The study investigated whether real-time fMRI neurofeedback facilitates anxiety regulation by cognitive reappraisal in females with spider phobia.

spans.text: The aim of this study was to investigate if providing neurofeedback during cognitive reappraisal would facilitate regulation success in spider phobia as a specific form of anxiety disorders.

description.value: Randomized, controlled, single-blinded study with neurofeedback and control groups.

spans.text: Eighteen female spider phobics participated in a randomized, controlled, single-blinded study.

functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI)
The 50-min imaging session started with one 5-min anatomical imaging run, followed by four 11-min functional imaging runs.
Images were acquired at Maastricht Brain Imaging Centre (Maastricht University) on a 3T scanner (Tim Trio/upgraded to Prisma Fit, Siemens Healthcare, Germany).

The functional echo-planar imaging (EPI) sequence was optimized for imaging of limbic and prefrontal regions (Weiskopf et al.,  2007 ; Morawetz et al.,  2008 ): repetition time = 1250 ms, echo time = 25 ms, flip angle = 67°, slice thickness = 2.5 mm, 20% gap, in-plane = 3 × 3 mm, slice angle of 25–30°, grappa acceleration = 2.

instructions.value: During regulate trials, participants used cognitive reappraisal to reinterpret the spider photograph by finding calming aspects, focusing on safety, and avoiding anxiety-provoking thoughts. They selected strategies involving detecting the spider's aesthetics, focusing on its powerlessness, humanizing it, or imagining it in a safe environment. During watch trials, they refrained from changing their thoughts and let thoughts occur spontaneously.

stimuli.value: Photographs of spiders, selected to become increasingly anxiety provoking across runs and presented once per condition.

spans.text: To keep the training challenging throughout the experiment, the presented stimuli were selected to be increasingly anxiety provoking with each run
